questions.q: Beyond a list of object names, what else does this lesson say real migration scope has to define?
options: Nothing else — object names are sufficient to define scope
Which fields per object are in scope, how far back historical data goes, and what's explicitly being left behind
Only the names of the Salesforce users who will perform the load
The exact CSV delimiter character to be used during the load
questions.explain: Real scope specifies in-scope fields per object, a historical date range, and an explicit, documented list of what's deliberately excluded — not just a bare object list.

questions.q: What is the main trade-off of a big-bang migration strategy compared to a phased strategy?
options: Big bang is always cheaper and carries no additional risk
Big bang requires both systems to run side by side indefinitely
Big bang only works for migrations with fewer than 1,000 records
Big bang is simpler to plan with one cutover, but concentrates all risk into a single event and usually needs a longer freeze window
questions.explain: Big bang is simpler to plan and reason about, but that simplicity comes from concentrating risk into one event and usually demanding a harder, longer freeze on the legacy system during the final load.

questions.q: What specific complexity does a phased (trickle) migration strategy introduce that big bang avoids?
options: The need for any field mapping at all
The requirement to migrate every object in a single event
Potentially having to run both systems side by side for a period, and handling relationships that span a stage boundary
The need for a data-quality scorecard, which big bang doesn't require
questions.explain: Phased migration spreads risk across smaller stages but can require legacy and target systems to coexist temporarily, and needs deliberate handling for relationships (like a migrated Contact whose Opportunity hasn't moved yet) that cross a stage boundary.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say scope sign-off needs to happen before design work starts, rather than being revisited casually later?
options: Because Chapter 2's mapping and transformation design, and Chapter 3's validation criteria, are built directly on top of the agreed scope
Because Salesforce technically prevents any design work from starting without a signed scope document
Because sign-off is a purely legal formality with no real effect on downstream work
Because scope sign-off is only required for phased migrations, not big-bang ones
questions.explain: If scope shifts after design work has started, mapping, transformation, and validation work already built on the original scope may have to be redone — sign-off exists specifically to prevent that costly rework.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say scope creep is particularly dangerous, as opposed to simply being an inconvenience?
options: Because any single scope addition is always technically impossible to accommodate
Because it typically happens mid-project, after mapping and transformation work has already started against the original, smaller scope
Because scope creep only ever affects the final cutover date and nothing else
Because it always doubles the total number of objects in scope
questions.explain: Scope creep's danger comes from timing: each 'small' addition risks invalidating mapping, sequencing, or even rehearsal work already built assuming the original scope — which is why disciplined projects treat it as a formal change request, not a free favor.
